question.text: During the reign of this emperor, the siege of the Masada ended the First Jewish Revolt. This emperor is said to have fiddled during the Great Fire of Rome.
question.clue: This leader's mother Agrippina the Younger was initially his regent, but he eventually had her assassinated.

swap.leadin: A period of expansion into Germany under this ruler was ended by defeat at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest.
swap.text: Name this first Emperor of Rome, who conquered Egypt through victory at the Battle of Actium.
swap.answerHtml: Octavian [or Augustus Caesar or Gaius Octavius; do not accept or prompt on just “Caesar”]
swap.clue: The Second Triumvirate consisted of Antony, Lepidus, and this adopted son of Julius Caesar, who fought a civil war against Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BCE and became the first Emperor of Rome.

question.leadin: Bridges are often important military objectives, as they can create chokepoints to slow an army's advance or retreat.
question.text: In 312 CE, Constantine I soundly defeated Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, which spans this major river of Rome. Maxentius drowned in this river's waters during the battle.
question.clue: The first colonia was a city at the mouth of this river which imported grain and was named Ostia.

swap.text: With Cleopatra, this triumvir commanded the losing army at Actium. This man killed himself thinking that Cleopatra was dead, which led to her suicide.
swap.clue: Cicero's head and hands were sent to this leader after Cicero attacked him in his writings and this man was defeated at the Battle of Actium.

question.leadin: The members of the First Triumvirate all had interesting deaths.
question.text: This man was stabbed on the floor of the Roman Senate by a team of rebellious senators. Following his victory in a civil war, this man convinced the Senate to declare him dictator for life, one month before his assassination.
question.clue: Notable images on this man's coins include an elephant fighting a snake and a jug and lituus, and he served his first consulship with Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus.

swap.text: After defeating him at the Battle of the Silarius River, Crassus ordered 6,000 followers of this gladiator to be crucified along the Appian Way, thus ending the Third Servile War.
swap.clue: After Crassus defeated this man, Pompey arrived from Spain and took credit for the victory.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about Roman priesthoods.
question.text: These Roman priestesses took thirty-year vows of chastity. The chief duty of these priestesses was to tend the eternal fire of Rome.
question.clue: These people oversaw rites during the Bona Dea festival.

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about historical events that appear in the worksof the Roman historian Tacitus.
swap.text: According to Tacitus, this ruler of the Iceni revolted against Roman rule after the death of Prasutagus. Suetonius Paulinus ultimately defeated this ruler near Paulerspury.
swap.clue: This person's popularity as a patriotic symbol in Victorian Britain was influenced by the theory that her name comes from a root meaning "victory" in Celtic.

question.leadin: Identify these other kings of Rome.
question.text: After his son raped the noblewoman Lucretia, this last king of Rome was driven out in 509 BC by a mob led by Junius Brutus and was forced into exile in Etruria.
question.answer: Tarquinius Superbus or Tarquin the Proud
question.clue: This Roman king overthrew Servius Tullius and was himself deposed after his son Sextus raped Lucretia, leading her kinsmen to rebel.

swap.leadin: He built the Cloaca Maxima and acquired the Sibylline books, but his son's crime and his overbearing demeanor led to his overthrow by Lucius Brutus.
swap.text: Name this last king of Rome, whose character was reflected in his cognomen.
swap.clue: This ruler took refuge with Aristodemus of Cumae after a battle in which Castor and Pollux purportedly fought against him.

question.leadin: This structure stretched 73 miles from Wallsend-on-Tyne to Solway Firth.
question.text: Identify this structure that was built by the Romans as a defense mechanism against barbarians in England. Begun in AD 122, its namesake emperor also dealt with the Bar Kokhba revolt in Judea.
question.clue: A birthday invitation was found on one of the Vindolanda tablets, which were unearthed near this structure.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about recipients of the Grass Crown, the highest and rarest military honor in ancient Rome.
swap.text: Quintus Sertorius was awarded the Grass Crown for putting down a rebellion in this region, where he would later launch his own rebellion. Emperor Theodosius the Great was born in this region.
swap.answerHtml: Hispania [accept Spain, Portugal, or anything referring to the Iberian peninsula]
swap.clue: Hasdrubal Gisco lost to a "reverse Cannae" at Ilipa ("ILL-ih-puh") in this region, which was later the location of the Numantine War.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about a Roman reformer.
question.text: The elder brother of Gaius Sempronius, this man and namsake of an agrarian reform law was killed in 133 in a riot precipitated by Nasica.
question.clue: This politician broke with precedent and twice tried to be elected tribune.

swap.text: Roman Senators were marked by having a purple stripe on this popular Roman garment, wrapped around the body, which includes the praetexta variety.
swap.clue: The praetexta variety of these semicircular items included a purple band and were used by magistrates.

question.leadin: Answer the following about attacks on Roman control in Hispania.
question.text: This former shepherd and leader of the Lusitani rose up against Roman control after a governor dug a trench around a group of Lusitani and killed them while they were surrendering their weapons. This leader defeated a Roman army at the Battle of Mt. Veneris.
question.clue: Polybius called the long struggle with this leader of the Lusitanians the "War of Fire" for its violence. Wildly successful against Rome on the battlefield, he was killed in his sleep by three bribed Tartessian assassins.

swap.leadin: In a poem describing God, he wrote that God "is indescribable" even to Jesus.
swap.text: Name this author of "Thalia" whose views were criticized by Athanasius (ath-uh-NAY-shus) in On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia (uh-RIM-in-um and si-LOO-shuh)
swap.clue: While speaking at an event, this person was apocryphally slapped by an outraged man from Patara.

question.text: This confederate of the lawyer Celestius wrote the tract On Free Will but was condemned by Pope Zosimus at the Council of Carthage for his belief in the ability of men to save themselves.
question.clue: This British heretic, who famously denied original sin and incurred the wrath of St. Augustine.

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about slavery in the ancient world.
swap.text: Although freed Roman slaves sometimes went on to become prominent merchants, they were barred from following this path, which began with serving as a tribune and culminated in the consulship.
swap.clue: This sequence of offices, through which a Roman magistrate rose in prominence.

question.text: Curzio Inghirami botched his staged discoveries of Etruscan "scariths" by using paper instead of this material. The Zagreb Book is an Etruscan text written on this material that was found wrapped around an Egyptian mummy.
question.answerHtml: linen [or flax; accept Liber Linteus, Libri lintei, or linen rolls; prompt on textiles, fabric, or synonyms]

swap.leadin: Answer the following about Orestes, the historical one, FTPE.
swap.text: Flavius Orestes deposed this Western Roman Emperor, sometimes considered the last emperor, in order to install his son Romulus Augustulus. This guy fled Ravenna and continued to reign in exile at Salona in Dalmatia until 480 CE.
